     2	
     3	## Source
     4	
     5	- URL: https://artificialanalysis.ai/

     7	
     8	Artificial Analysis is an independent platform that benchmarks large language models across intelligence, speed, and pricing. The data below reflects the latest evaluations published in April 2026, covering both proprietary and open-weight models from major AI labs worldwide.
     9	
    10	## Intelligence Index: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5.4 Share the Lead at 57
    11	
    12	The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is a composite score aggregating performance across a wide range of reasoning, knowledge, and instruction-following benchmarks. Higher scores indicate stronger overall capability.
    13	
    14	As of April 2026, two models share the top position:
    15	
    16	| Rank | Model | Provider | Intelligence Index |
    17	|------|-------|----------|--------------------|
    18	| 1 | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | Google | 57 |
    19	| 2 | GPT-5.4 (xhigh) | OpenAI | 57 |
    20	| 3 | Claude Opus 4.6 (max) | Anthropic | 53 |
    21	| 4 | Muse Spark | Meta | 52 |
    22	| 5 | Claude Sonnet 4.6 (max) | Anthropic | 52 |
    23	| 6 | GLM-5.1 | Z AI | 51 |
    24	| 7 | Grok 4.20 0309 v2 | xAI | 49 |
    25	| 8 | Gemini 3 Flash | Google | 46 |
    26	| 9 | DeepSeek V3.2 | DeepSeek | 42 |
    27	| 10 | NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super | NVIDIA | 36 |
    28	| 11 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | OpenAI | 33 |
    29	
    30	Google and OpenAI are neck-and-neck at the frontier. Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 trails by 4 points, while Meta's newly released Muse Spark enters at a strong 52. Open-weight models such as GLM-5.1 and Grok 4.20 occupy the mid-tier, demonstrating that the gap between proprietary and open-weight models continues to narrow.
    31	
    32	![Intelligence Index ranking of top AI models, April 2026](./assets/chart_intelligence_index_ranking.jpg)
    33	
    34	## Output Speed: Open-Weight Models Dominate Throughput
    35	
    36	Inference speed, measured in output tokens per second, is critical for latency-sensitive applications. The leaderboard shows a striking pattern: open-weight and smaller models generate tokens far faster than frontier proprietary models.
    37	
    38	| Rank | Model | Output Tokens/s |
    39	|------|-------|-----------------|
    40	| 1 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | 218 |
    41	| 2 | Grok 4.20 0309 v2 | 188 |
    42	| 3 | NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super | 172 |
    43	| 4 | Gemini 3 Flash | 153 |
    44	| 5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | 118 |
    45	| 6 | GPT-5.4 (xhigh) | 83 |
    46	| 7 | GLM-5.1 | 64 |
    47	| 8 | Claude Sonnet 4.6 (max) | 63 |
    48	| 9 | Claude Opus 4.6 (max) | 49 |
    49	| 10 | DeepSeek V3.2 | 46 |
    50	
    51	The fastest model, gpt-oss-120B (high), outputs 218 tokens per second -- more than 4x the speed of Claude Opus 4.6 and nearly 5x that of DeepSeek V3.2. This highlights the trade-off between raw intelligence and throughput: the two intelligence leaders (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5.4) sit in the middle of the speed table at 118 and 83 tokens/s respectively.
    52	
    53	![Output speed ranking by tokens per second](./assets/chart_output_speed_ranking.jpg)
    54	
    55	## Pricing: A 33x Gap Between Cheapest and Most Expensive
    56	
    57	API pricing per million tokens varies enormously across models, reflecting differences in compute requirements, margin strategies, and competitive positioning.
    58	
    59	| Rank | Model | USD per 1M Tokens |
    60	|------|-------|--------------------|
    61	| 1 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | $0.30 |
    62	| 2 | DeepSeek V3.2 | $0.30 |
    63	| 3 | NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super | $0.40 |
    64	| 4 | Gemini 3 Flash | $1.10 |
    65	| 5 | GLM-5.1 | $2.10 |
    66	| 6 | Grok 4.20 0309 v2 | $3.00 |
    67	| 7 | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | $4.50 |
    68	| 8 | GPT-5.4 (xhigh) | $5.60 |
    69	| 9 | Claude Sonnet 4.6 (max) | $6.00 |
    70	| 10 | Claude Opus 4.6 (max) | $10.00 |
    71	
    72	The cheapest options -- gpt-oss-120B and DeepSeek V3.2 at $0.30 per million tokens -- are over 33x less expensive than Claude Opus 4.6 at $10.00. For budget-sensitive workloads, this price differential is a decisive factor. Notably, Gemini 3 Flash offers a compelling mid-range value at $1.10, pairing solid speed (153 tokens/s) with reasonable intelligence (46).
    73	
    74	![Price per million tokens comparison across models](./assets/chart_price_per_million_tokens.jpg)
    75	
    76	## The Intelligence-Throughput Frontier: Finding the "Most Attractive Quadrant"
    77	
    78	A scatter plot of Intelligence Index versus output tokens consumed during evaluation reveals which models occupy the "most attractive quadrant" -- high intelligence with efficient token usage. Models that achieve high scores while consuming fewer tokens represent better engineering and more efficient architectures.
    79	
    80	Key observations from the scatter plot:
    81	
    82	- Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and DeepSeek V3.2 cluster in the upper region, indicating strong intelligence scores.
    83	- Grok 4.20 0309 v2 and several Google models sit in the middle-right region, balancing intelligence and token efficiency.
    84	- Llama 4 Maverick occupies the low-intelligence, low-token region, suggesting it is neither efficient nor highly capable.
    85	- MiMo-V2-Pro appears in the upper-right corner, showing very high intelligence but with substantial token usage.
    86	
    87	![Scatter plot of intelligence index vs output tokens, highlighting the most attractive quadrant](./assets/chart_intelligence_vs_output_tokens.jpg)
    88	
    89	## Proprietary vs. Open-Weight Models
    90	
    91	The April 2026 landscape shows proprietary models still leading on raw intelligence, but the margin is thin. GLM-5.1, an open-weight model from Z AI, scores 51 -- just 6 points behind the co-leaders. Meanwhile, open-weight models like gpt-oss-120B dominate on speed and price. The intelligence leaderboard includes models from at least 8 distinct organizations across the US, China, and Europe, reflecting a genuinely global competition.
    92	
    93	| Metric | Proprietary Leader | Score | Open-Weight Leader | Score |
    94	|--------|--------------------|-------|--------------------|-------|
    95	| Intelligence | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | 57 | GLM-5.1 | 51 |
    96	| Speed (tokens/s) | Gemini 3 Flash | 153 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | 218 |
    97	| Price ($/1M tokens) | Gemini 3 Flash | $1.10 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | $0.30 |
    98	
    99	## Key Findings
   100	
   101	- **Two-way tie at the top**: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5.4 (xhigh) both score 57 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, making them the co-leaders as of April 2026.
   102	- **Speed and intelligence are inversely correlated**: The fastest model (gpt-oss-120B at 218 tokens/s) scores only 33 on intelligence, while the smartest models operate at 49-118 tokens/s.
   103	- **Massive pricing spread**: A 33x cost gap separates the cheapest ($0.30/1M tokens for gpt-oss-120B and DeepSeek V3.2) from the most expensive ($10.00/1M tokens for Claude Opus 4.6).
   104	- **Open-weight models are closing the gap**: GLM-5.1 at 51 intelligence is within 10% of the proprietary leaders, while also being significantly cheaper at $2.10/1M tokens.
   105	- **No single model wins on all three axes**: Choosing a model requires explicit trade-offs among intelligence, speed, and cost depending on the use case.

     2	name: frontend-slides
     3	description: Create stunning, animation-rich HTML presentations from scratch or by converting PowerPoint files. Use when the user wants to build a presentation, convert a PPT/PPTX to web, or create slides for a talk/pitch. Helps non-designers discover their aesthetic through visual exploration rather than abstract choices.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Frontend Slides
     7	
     8	Create zero-dependency, animation-rich HTML presentations that run entirely in the browser.
     9	
    10	## Core Principles
    11	
    12	1. **Zero Dependencies** — Single HTML files with inline CSS/JS. No npm, no build tools.
    13	2. **Show, Don't Tell** — Generate visual previews, not abstract choices. People discover what they want by seeing it.
    14	3. **Distinctive Design** — No generic "AI slop." Every presentation must feel custom-crafted.
    15	4. **Viewport Fitting (NON-NEGOTIABLE)** — Every slide MUST fit exactly within 100vh. No scrolling within slides, ever. Content overflows? Split into multiple slides.
    16	
    17	## Design Aesthetics
    18	
    19	You tend to converge toward generic, "on distribution" outputs. In frontend design, this creates what users call the "AI slop" aesthetic. Avoid this: make creative, distinctive frontends that surprise and delight.
    20	
    21	Focus on:
    22	
    23	- Typography: Choose fonts that are beautiful, unique, and interesting. Avoid generic fonts like Arial and Inter; opt instead for distinctive choices that elevate the frontend's aesthetics.
    24	- Color & Theme: Commit to a cohesive aesthetic. Use CSS variables for consistency. Dominant colors with sharp accents outperform timid, evenly-distributed palettes. Draw from IDE themes and cultural aesthetics for inspiration.
    25	- Motion: Use animations for effects and micro-interactions. Prioritize CSS-only solutions for HTML. Use Motion library for React when available. Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered micro-interactions.
    26	- Backgrounds: Create atmosphere and depth rather than defaulting to solid colors. Layer CSS gradients, use geometric patterns, or add contextual effects that match the overall aesthetic.
    27	
    28	Avoid generic AI-generated aesthetics:
    29	
    30	- Overused font families (Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts)
    31	- Cliched color schemes (particularly purple gradients on white backgrounds)
    32	- Predictable layouts and component patterns
    33	- Cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character
    34	
    35	Interpret creatively and make unexpected choices that feel genuinely designed for the context. Vary between light and dark themes, different fonts, different aesthetics. You still tend to converge on common choices (Space Grotesk, for example) across generations. Avoid this: it is critical that you think outside the box!
    36	
    37	## Viewport Fitting Rules
    38	
    39	These invariants apply to EVERY slide in EVERY presentation:
    40	
    41	- Every `.slide` must have `height: 100vh; height: 100dvh; overflow: hidden;`
    42	- ALL font sizes and spacing must use `clamp(min, preferred, max)` — never fixed px/rem
    43	- Content containers need `max-height` constraints
    44	- Images: `max-height: min(50vh, 400px)`
    45	- Breakpoints required for heights: 700px, 600px, 500px
    46	- Include `prefers-reduced-motion` support
    47	- Never negate CSS functions directly (`-clamp()`, `-min()`, `-max()` are silently ignored) — use `calc(-1 * clamp(...))` instead
    48	
    49	**When generating, read `viewport-base.css` and include its full contents in every presentation.**
    50	
    51	### Content Density Limits Per Slide
    52	
    53	| Slide Type    | Maximum Content                                           |
    54	| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
    55	| Title slide   | 1 heading + 1 subtitle + optional tagline                 |
    56	| Content slide | 1 heading + 4-6 bullet points OR 1 heading + 2 paragraphs |
    57	| Feature grid  | 1 heading + 6 cards maximum (2x3 or 3x2)                  |
    58	| Code slide    | 1 heading + 8-10 lines of code                            |
    59	| Quote slide   | 1 quote (max 3 lines) + attribution                       |
    60	| Image slide   | 1 heading + 1 image (max 60vh height)                     |
    61	
    62	**Content exceeds limits? Split into multiple slides. Never cram, never scroll.**
    63	
    64	---
    65	
    66	## Phase 0: Detect Mode
    67	
    68	Determine what the user wants:
    69	
    70	- **Mode A: New Presentation** — Create from scratch. Go to Phase 1.
    71	- **Mode B: PPT Conversion** — Convert a .pptx file. Go to Phase 4.
    72	- **Mode C: Enhancement** — Improve an existing HTML presentation. Read it, understand it, enhance. **Follow Mode C modification rules below.**
    73	
    74	### Mode C: Modification Rules
    75	
    76	When enhancing existing presentations, viewport fitting is the biggest risk:
    77	
    78	1. **Before adding content:** Count existing elements, check against density limits
    79	2. **Adding images:** Must have `max-height: min(50vh, 400px)`. If slide already has max content, split into two slides
    80	3. **Adding text:** Max 4-6 bullets per slide. Exceeds limits? Split into continuation slides
    81	4. **After ANY modification, verify:** `.slide` has `overflow: hidden`, new elements use `clamp()`, images have viewport-relative max-height, content fits at 1280x720
    82	5. **Proactively reorganize:** If modifications will cause overflow, automatically split content and inform the user. Don't wait to be asked
    83	
    84	**When adding images to existing slides:** Move image to new slide or reduce other content first. Never add images without checking if existing content already fills the viewport.
    85	
    86	---
    87	
    88	## Phase 1: Content Discovery (New Presentations)
    89	
    90	**Ask ALL questions in a single AskUserQuestion call** so the user fills everything out at once:
    91	
    92	**Question 1 — Purpose** (header: "Purpose"):
    93	What is this presentation for? Options: Pitch deck / Teaching-Tutorial / Conference talk / Internal presentation
    94	
    95	**Question 2 — Length** (header: "Length"):
    96	Approximately how many slides? Options: Short 5-10 / Medium 10-20 / Long 20+
    97	
    98	**Question 3 — Content** (header: "Content"):
    99	Do you have content ready? Options: All content ready / Rough notes / Topic only
   100	
   101	**Question 4 — Inline Editing** (header: "Editing"):
   102	Do you need to edit text directly in the browser after generation? Options:
   103	
   104	- "Yes (Recommended)" — Can edit text in-browser, auto-save to localStorage, export file
   105	- "No" — Presentation only, keeps file smaller
   106	
   107	**Remember the user's editing choice — it determines whether edit-related code is included in Phase 3.**
   108	
   109	If user has content, ask them to share it.
   110	
   111	### Step 1.2: Image Evaluation (if images provided)
   112	
   113	If user selected "No images" → skip to Phase 2.
   114	
   115	If user provides an image folder:
   116	
   117	1. **Scan** — List all image files (.png, .jpg, .svg, .webp, etc.)
   118	2. **View each image** — Use the Read tool (Claude is multimodal)
   119	3. **Evaluate** — For each: what it shows, USABLE or NOT USABLE (with reason), what concept it represents, dominant colors
   120	4. **Co-design the outline** — Curated images inform slide structure alongside text. This is NOT "plan slides then add images" — design around both from the start (e.g., 3 screenshots → 3 feature slides, 1 logo → title/closing slide)
   121	5. **Confirm via AskUserQuestion** (header: "Outline"): "Does this slide outline and image selection look right?" Options: Looks good / Adjust images / Adjust outline
   122	
   123	**Logo in previews:** If a usable logo was identified, embed it (base64) into each style preview in Phase 2 — the user sees their brand styled three different ways.
   124	
   125	---
   126	
   127	## Phase 2: Style Discovery
   128	
   129	**This is the "show, don't tell" phase.** Most people can't articulate design preferences in words.
   130	
   131	### Step 2.0: Style Path
   132	
   133	Ask how they want to choose (header: "Style"):
   134	
   135	- "Show me options" (recommended) — Generate 3 previews based on mood
   136	- "I know what I want" — Pick from preset list directly
   137	
   138	**If direct selection:** Show preset picker and skip to Phase 3. Available presets are defined in [STYLE_PRESETS.md](STYLE_PRESETS.md).
   139	
   140	### Step 2.1: Mood Selection (Guided Discovery)
   141	
   142	Ask (header: "Vibe", multiSelect: true, max 2):
   143	What feeling should the audience have? Options:
   144	
   145	- Impressed/Confident — Professional, trustworthy
   146	- Excited/Energized — Innovative, bold
   147	- Calm/Focused — Clear, thoughtful
   148	- Inspired/Moved — Emotional, memorable
   149	
   150	### Step 2.2: Generate 3 Style Previews
   151	
   152	Based on mood, generate 3 distinct single-slide HTML previews showing typography, colors, animation, and overall aesthetic. Read [STYLE_PRESETS.md](STYLE_PRESETS.md) for available presets and their specifications.
   153	
   154	| Mood                | Suggested Presets                                  |
   155	| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
   156	| Impressed/Confident | Bold Signal, Electric Studio, Dark Botanical       |
   157	| Excited/Energized   | Creative Voltage, Neon Cyber, Split Pastel         |
   158	| Calm/Focused        | Notebook Tabs, Paper & Ink, Swiss Modern           |
   159	| Inspired/Moved      | Dark Botanical, Vintage Editorial, Pastel Geometry |
   160	
   161	Save previews to `.claude-design/slide-previews/` (style-a.html, style-b.html, style-c.html). Each should be self-contained, ~50-100 lines, showing one animated title slide.
   162	
   163	Open each preview automatically for the user.
   164	
   165	### Step 2.3: User Picks
   166	
   167	Ask (header: "Style"):
   168	Which style preview do you prefer? Options: Style A: [Name] / Style B: [Name] / Style C: [Name] / Mix elements
   169	
   170	If "Mix elements", ask for specifics.
   171	
   172	---
   173	
   174	## Phase 3: Generate Presentation
   175	
   176	Generate the full presentation using content from Phase 1 (text, or text + curated images) and style from Phase 2.
   177	
   178	If images were provided, the slide outline already incorporates them from Step 1.2. If not, CSS-generated visuals (gradients, shapes, patterns) provide visual interest — this is a fully supported first-class path.
   179	
   180	**Before generating, read these supporting files:**
   181	
   182	- [html-template.md](html-template.md) — HTML architecture and JS features
   183	- [viewport-base.css](viewport-base.css) — Mandatory CSS (include in full)
   184	- [animation-patterns.md](animation-patterns.md) — Animation reference for the chosen feeling
   185	
   186	**Key requirements:**
   187	
   188	- Single self-contained HTML file, all CSS/JS inline
   189	- Include the FULL contents of viewport-base.css in the `<style>` block
   190	- Use fonts from Fontshare or Google Fonts — never system fonts
   191	- Add detailed comments explaining each section
   192	- Every section needs a clear `/* === SECTION NAME === */` comment block
   193	
   194	---
   195	
   196	## Phase 4: PPT Conversion
   197	
   198	When converting PowerPoint files:
   199	
   200	1. **Extract content** — Run `python scripts/extract-pptx.py <input.pptx> <output_dir>` (install python-pptx if needed: `pip install python-pptx`)
   201	2. **Confirm with user** — Present extracted slide titles, content summaries, and image counts
   202	3. **Style selection** — Proceed to Phase 2 for style discovery
   203	4. **Generate HTML** — Convert to chosen style, preserving all text, images (from assets/), slide order, and speaker notes (as HTML comments)
   204	
   205	---
   206	
   207	## Phase 5: Delivery
   208	
   209	1. **Clean up** — Delete `.claude-design/slide-previews/` if it exists
   210	2. **Convert to PPTX** — Run the conversion script to produce a PowerPoint file:
   211	   ```bash
   212	   python scripts/html_to_pptx.py <presentation.html> /app/output/final_deck.pptx
   213	   ```
   214	   This starts a local HTTP server, uses Playwright to screenshot each slide at 1920×1080, and assembles the images into a 16:9 PPTX. The PPTX slides are full-bleed images — text is not editable, but the visual fidelity matches the HTML exactly.
   215	3. **Open** — Use `open [filename].html` to launch in browser
   216	4. **Summarize** — Tell the user:
   217	   - File location, style name, slide count
   218	   - Navigation: Arrow keys, Space, scroll/swipe, click nav dots
   219	   - How to customize: `:root` CSS variables for colors, font link for typography, `.reveal` class for animations
   220	   - If inline editing was enabled: Hover top-left corner or press E to enter edit mode, click any text to edit, Ctrl+S to save
   221	
   222	---
   223	
   224	## Phase 6: Share & Export (Optional)
   225	
   226	After delivery, **ask the user:** _"Would you like to share this presentation? I can deploy it to a live URL (works on any device including phones) or export it as a PDF."_
   227	
   228	Options:
   229	
   230	- **Deploy to URL** — Shareable link that works on any device
   231	- **Export to PDF** — Universal file for email, Slack, print
   232	- **Both**
   233	- **No thanks**
   234	
   235	If the user declines, stop here. If they choose one or both, proceed below.
   236	
   237	### 6A: Deploy to a Live URL (Vercel)
   238	
   239	This deploys the presentation to Vercel — a free hosting platform. The link works on any device (phones, tablets, laptops) and stays live until the user takes it down.
   240	
   241	**If the user has never deployed before, guide them step by step:**
   242	
   243	1. **Check if Vercel CLI is installed** — Run `npx vercel --version`. If not found, install Node.js first (`brew install node` on macOS, or download from https://nodejs.org).
   244	
   245	2. **Check if user is logged in** — Run `npx vercel whoami`.
   246	   - If NOT logged in, explain: _"Vercel is a free hosting service. You need an account to deploy. Let me walk you through it:"_
   247	     - Step 1: Ask user to go to https://vercel.com/signup in their browser
   248	     - Step 2: They can sign up with GitHub, Google, email — whatever is easiest
   249	     - Step 3: Once signed up, run `vercel login` and follow the prompts (it opens a browser window to authorize)
   250	     - Step 4: Confirm login with `vercel whoami`
   251	   - Wait for the user to confirm they're logged in before proceeding.
   252	
   253	3. **Deploy** — Run the deploy script:
   254	
   255	   ```bash
   256	   bash scripts/deploy.sh <path-to-presentation>
   257	   ```
   258	
   259	   The script accepts either a folder (with index.html) or a single HTML file.
   260	
   261	4. **Share the URL** — Tell the user:
   262	   - The live URL (from the script output)
   263	   - That it works on any device — they can text it, Slack it, email it
   264	   - To take it down later: visit https://vercel.com/dashboard and delete the project
   265	   - The Vercel free tier is generous — they won't be charged
   266	
   267	**⚠ Deployment gotchas:**
   268	
   269	- **Local images/videos must travel with the HTML.** The deploy script auto-detects files referenced via `src="..."` in the HTML and bundles them. But if the presentation references files via CSS `background-image` or unusual paths, those may be missed. **Before deploying, verify:** open the deployed URL and check that all images load. If any are broken, the safest fix is to put the HTML and all its assets into a single folder and deploy the folder instead of a standalone HTML file.
   270	- **Prefer folder deployments when the presentation has many assets.** If the presentation lives in a folder with images alongside it (e.g., `my-deck/index.html` + `my-deck/logo.png`), deploy the folder directly: `bash scripts/deploy.sh ./my-deck/`. This is more reliable than deploying a single HTML file because the entire folder contents are uploaded as-is.
   271	- **Filenames with spaces work but can cause issues.** The script handles spaces in filenames, but Vercel URLs encode spaces as `%20`. If possible, avoid spaces in image filenames. If the user's images have spaces, the script handles it — but if images still break, renaming files to use hyphens instead of spaces is the fix.
   272	- **Redeploying updates the same URL.** Running the deploy script again on the same presentation overwrites the previous deployment. The URL stays the same — no need to share a new link.
   273	
   274	### 6B: Export to PDF
   275	
   276	This captures each slide as a screenshot and combines them into a PDF. Perfect for email attachments, embedding in documents, or printing.
   277	
   278	**Note:** Animations and interactivity are not preserved — the PDF is a static snapshot. This is normal and expected; mention it to the user so they're not surprised.
   279	
   280	1. **Run the export script:**
   281	
   282	   ```bash
   283	   bash scripts/export-pdf.sh <path-to-html> [output.pdf]
   284	   ```
   285	
   286	   If no output path is given, the PDF is saved next to the HTML file.
   287	
   288	2. **What happens behind the scenes** (explain briefly to the user):
   289	   - A headless browser opens the presentation at 1920×1080 (standard widescreen)
   290	   - It screenshots each slide one by one
   291	   - All screenshots are combined into a single PDF
   292	   - The script needs Playwright (a browser automation tool) — it will install automatically if missing
   293	
   294	3. **If Playwright installation fails:**
   295	   - The most common issue is Chromium not downloading. Run: `npx playwright install chromium`
   296	   - If that fails too, it may be a network/firewall issue. Ask the user to try on a different network.
   297	
   298	4. **Deliver the PDF** — The script auto-opens it. Tell the user:
   299	   - The file location and size
   300	   - That it works everywhere — email, Slack, Notion, Google Docs, print
   301	   - Animations are replaced by their final visual state (still looks great, just static)
   302	
   303	**⚠ PDF export gotchas:**
   304	
   305	- **First run is slow.** The script installs Playwright and downloads a Chromium browser (~150MB) into a temp directory. This happens once per run. Warn the user it may take 30-60 seconds the first time — subsequent exports within the same session are faster.
   306	- **Slides must use `class="slide"`.** The export script finds slides by querying `.slide` elements. If the presentation uses a different class name, the script will report "0 slides found" and fail. All presentations generated by this skill use `.slide`, so this only matters for externally-created HTML.
   307	- **Local images must be loadable via HTTP.** The script starts a local server and loads the HTML through it (so Google Fonts and relative image paths work). If images use absolute filesystem paths (e.g., `src="/Users/name/photo.png"`) instead of relative paths (e.g., `src="photo.png"`), they won't load. Generated presentations always use relative paths, but converted or user-provided decks might not — check and fix if needed.
   308	- **Local images appear in the PDF** as long as they are in the same directory as (or relative to) the HTML file. The export script serves the HTML's parent directory over HTTP, so relative paths like `src="photo.png"` resolve correctly — including filenames with spaces. If images still don't appear, check: (1) the image files actually exist at the referenced path, (2) the paths are relative, not absolute filesystem paths like `/Users/name/photo.png`.
   309	- **Large presentations produce large PDFs.** Each slide is captured as a full 1920×1080 PNG screenshot. An 18-slide deck can produce a ~20MB PDF. If the PDF exceeds 10MB, ask the user: _"The PDF is [size]. Would you like me to compress it? It'll look slightly less sharp but the file will be much smaller."_ If yes, re-run the export with the `--compact` flag:
   310	  ```bash

   330	## CSS Gotchas
   331	
   332	### Negating CSS Functions
   333	
   334	**WRONG — silently ignored by browsers (no console error):**
   335	```css
   336	right: -clamp(28px, 3.5vw, 44px);   /* Browser ignores this */
   337	margin-left: -min(10vw, 100px);      /* Browser ignores this */
   338	```
   339	
   340	**CORRECT — wrap in `calc()`:**
   341	```css
   342	right: calc(-1 * clamp(28px, 3.5vw, 44px));  /* Works */
   343	margin-left: calc(-1 * min(10vw, 100px));     /* Works */
   344	```
   345	
   346	CSS does not allow a leading `-` before function names. The browser silently discards the entire declaration — no error, the element just appears in the wrong position. **Always use `calc(-1 * ...)` to negate CSS function values.**

     3

     5	the presentation, taking a full-viewport screenshot of each slide, then
     6	assemble the images into a 16:9 PPTX via python-pptx.
     7	
     8	A local HTTP server is started so Google Fonts and relative asset paths load
     9	correctly (file:// protocol blocks cross-origin font requests).

    11	Usage:
    12	    python html_to_pptx.py <input.html> <output.pptx> [--width 1920] [--height 1080]

    16	import os
    17	import http.server
    18	import subprocess

    21	import threading
    22	from pathlib import Path
    23	
    24	from PIL import Image

    28	
    29	# CSS selectors to count slides, tried in order
    30	SLIDE_SELECTORS = [".slide", "[data-slide]", "section", "div > section"]
    31	
    32	
    33	def _make_screenshot_script(url: str, out_dir: str, width: int, height: int) -> str:
    34	    """Return a Node.js script that navigates and screenshots each slide."""
    35	    selectors_js = ", ".join(f'"{s}"' for s in SLIDE_SELECTORS)
    36	    return f"""\
    37	const {{ chromium }} = require('playwright');
    38	
    39	(async () => {{
    40	    const browser = await chromium.launch({{ executablePath: process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH || undefined }});
    41	    const page = await browser.newPage();
    42	    await page.setViewportSize({{ width: {width}, height: {height} }});
    43	    await page.goto('{url}', {{ waitUntil: 'networkidle' }});
    44	
    45	    // --- Count slides using DOM selectors ---
    46	    const selectors = [{selectors_js}];
    47	    let slideCount = 0;
    48	    for (const sel of selectors) {{
    49	        slideCount = await page.$$eval(sel, els => els.length);
    50	        if (slideCount > 0) break;
    51	    }}
    52	
    53	    // Fallback: treat the whole page as 1 slide
    54	    if (slideCount === 0) slideCount = 1;
    55	
    56	    // Reasonable upper bound to prevent infinite loops
    57	    if (slideCount > 100) slideCount = 100;
    58	
    59	    // --- Capture slide 1 (already visible on load) ---
    60	    // Wait for entrance animations to settle
    61	    await page.waitForTimeout(500);
    62	    await page.screenshot({{ path: `{out_dir}/slide_001.png` }});
    63	
    64	    // --- Navigate through remaining slides via ArrowRight ---
    65	    // We track visual changes to detect when navigation has no more effect
    66	    // (i.e. we've passed the last slide).
    67	    let prevPath = `{out_dir}/slide_001.png`;
    68	    let captured = 1;
    69	
    70	    for (let i = 2; i <= slideCount; i++) {{
    71	        await page.keyboard.press('ArrowRight');
    72	        // Wait for transition animation to complete
    73	        await page.waitForTimeout(600);
    74	
    75	        const idx = String(i).padStart(3, '0');
    76	        const path = `{out_dir}/slide_${{idx}}.png`;
    77	        await page.screenshot({{ path }});
    78	        captured++;

    81	    console.log(JSON.stringify({{ captured }}));
    82	    await browser.close();
    83	}})();

    86	
    87	def _deduplicate_slides(image_dir: Path) -> list[Path]:
    88	    """Remove trailing duplicate screenshots (navigation past last slide).
    89	
    90	    Some presentations keep showing the last slide when you press ArrowRight
    91	    beyond the end.  We detect this by comparing file sizes + pixel samples.
    92	    """
    93	    pngs = sorted(image_dir.glob("slide_*.png"))
    94	    if len(pngs) <= 1:
    95	        return pngs
    96	
    97	    unique: list[Path] = [pngs[0]]
    98	    prev_img = Image.open(pngs[0])
    99	
   100	    for png in pngs[1:]:
   101	        curr_img = Image.open(png)
   102	        # Quick check: compare a grid of sample pixels
   103	        is_dup = True
   104	        for x_frac in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75):
   105	            for y_frac in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75):
   106	                px = int(curr_img.width * x_frac)
   107	                py = int(curr_img.height * y_frac)
   108	                if curr_img.getpixel((px, py)) != prev_img.getpixel((px, py)):
   109	                    is_dup = False
   110	                    break
   111	            if not is_dup:
   112	                break
   113	
   114	        if not is_dup:
   115	            unique.append(png)
   116	            prev_img = curr_img
   117	        else:
   118	            # Once we hit a duplicate, stop — remaining are likely all dupes
   119	            break
   120	
   121	    return unique

   124	def _start_http_server(directory: Path, port: int = 0):
   125	    """Start a background HTTP server serving *directory*. Returns (server, port)."""
   126	    handler = http.server.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler
   127	    server = http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), lambda *a, **kw: handler(*a, directory=str(directory), **kw))
   128	    actual_port = server.server_address[1]
   129	    thread = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)

   143	        script_file = out_dir / "_capture.cjs"

   145

        class SlidePresentation {
            constructor() {
                this.slides = document.querySelectorAll('.slide');
                this.currentSlide = 0;
                this.setupIntersectionObserver();
                this.setupKeyboardNav();
                this.setupTouchNav();
                this.setupProgressBar();
                this.setupNavDots();
                this.setupWheelNav();
            }

            setupIntersectionObserver() {
                const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
                    entries.forEach(entry => {
                        if (entry.isIntersecting) {
                            entry.target.classList.add('visible');
                            const idx = Array.from(this.slides).indexOf(entry.target);
                            this.currentSlide = idx;
                            this.updateProgressBar();
                            this.updateNavDots();
                        }
                    });
                }, { threshold: 0.5 });
                this.slides.forEach(slide => observer.observe(slide));
            }

            setupKeyboardNav() {
                document.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
                    if (e.key === 'ArrowDown' || e.key === 'ArrowRight' || e.key === ' ' || e.key === 'PageDown') {
                        e.preventDefault();
                        this.nextSlide();
                    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp' || e.key === 'ArrowLeft' || e.key === 'PageUp') {
                        e.preventDefault();
                        this.prevSlide();
                    } else if (e.key === 'Home') {
                        e.preventDefault();
                        this.goToSlide(0);
                    } else if (e.key === 'End') {
                        e.preventDefault();
                        this.goToSlide(this.slides.length - 1);
                    }
                });
            }

            setupTouchNav() {
                let startY = 0;
                document.addEventListener('touchstart', (e) => { startY = e.touches[0].clientY; });
                document.addEventListener('touchend', (e) => {
                    const endY = e.changedTouches[0].clientY;
                    const diff = startY - endY;
                    if (Math.abs(diff) > 50) {
                        diff > 0 ? this.nextSlide() : this.prevSlide();
                    }
                });
            }

            setupWheelNav() {
                let wheelTimeout = null;
                let accumulated = 0;
                document.addEventListener('wheel', (e) => {
                    e.preventDefault();
                    accumulated += e.deltaY;
                    if (wheelTimeout) return;
                    wheelTimeout = setTimeout(() => {
                        if (accumulated > 30) this.nextSlide();
                        else if (accumulated < -30) this.prevSlide();
                        accumulated = 0;
                        wheelTimeout = null;
                    }, 120);
                }, { passive: false });
            }

            setupProgressBar() {
                this.progressBar = document.getElementById('progressBar');
            }

            updateProgressBar() {
                if (!this.progressBar) return;
                const pct = ((this.currentSlide + 1) / this.slides.length) * 100;
                this.progressBar.style.width = pct + '%';
            }

            setupNavDots() {
                const nav = document.getElementById('navDots');
                if (!nav) return;
                this.slides.forEach((_, i) => {
                    const btn = document.createElement('button');
                    btn.className = 'nav-dot' + (i === 0 ? ' active' : '');
                    btn.setAttribute('aria-label', `Go to slide ${i + 1}`);
                    btn.addEventListener('click', () => this.goToSlide(i));
                    nav.appendChild(btn);
                });
                this.navDots = nav.querySelectorAll('.nav-dot');
            }

            updateNavDots() {
                if (!this.navDots) return;
                this.navDots.forEach((dot, i) => {
                    dot.classList.toggle('active', i === this.currentSlide);
                });
            }

            nextSlide() {
                if (this.currentSlide < this.slides.length - 1) {
                    this.goToSlide(this.currentSlide + 1);
                }
            }

            prevSlide() {
                if (this.currentSlide > 0) {
                    this.goToSlide(this.currentSlide - 1);
                }
            }

            goToSlide(index) {
                if (index >= 0 && index < this.slides.length) {
                    this.slides[index].scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' });
                }
            }
        }

        new SlidePresentation();
